newsitem.title: BOSNIA: West may suspend contacts with Bosnia ambassadors.
newsitem.headline: West may suspend contacts with Bosnia ambassadors.

text.p: Western governments might suspend contacts with Bosnia's ambassadors abroad unless the Bosnian government agrees soon on a law governing ambassadorial posts.

The international community's High Representative in Bosnia Carlos Westendorp told reporters on Saturday he had recommended to Western powers that no ambassador be treated as a legitimate representative of Bosnia until the law was agreed.

Western allies had threatened to impose penalties on the joint postwar government of Bosnia unless it reached agreement on three key laws by Friday -- a deadline set by NATO at a summit in May in Sintra, Portugal.

But Westendorp said he had extended the deadline until Monday because on two of the laws, governing passports and citizenship, good progress had been made. Bosnia's factions remain at loggerheads on a third measure to settle how ambassadorial posts should be divided among Serbs, Croats, Moslems and others.
"That's why we need to give it some more time. I am stopping the watch until Monday...It's just realism," he told a news conference.
He is not able to impose the penalty himself, but can only recommend action to national governments.
"The measures are not to deal with ambassadors who do not represent the country as a whole," he said.

Westendorp said that for Bosnia's ambassadors to become legitimate, agreement was needed between the country's rival ethnic groups. "As from that moment, they will be legitimate representatives of the state," he said.
His office said he had sent a letter to foreign capitals on Saturday recommending they suspend contacts with Bosnian ambassadors immediate effect until a solution was reached.
A Bosnian government official said that of Bosnia's diplomatic posts abroad, the ambassadorship in Washington was the most hotly disputed among rival ethnic groups.

However he said the Moslems were prepared to compromise by offering the post to someone who was neither Serb, Croat nor Moslem, but belonged to the 8.7 percent of Bosnians considered to belong to other ethnic groups.

Westendorp said the members of the Contact Group on former Yugoslavia -- France, Britain, Germany, Russia and the United States -- were asking him for action but he didn't want to impose "too many penalties".
"I prefer positive action to punishing people," he said.

If agreement is not reached on passport and citizenship issues on Monday, Westendorp said the easiest way to sanction Sarajevo would be by not recognising travel documents or passports, "not of everyone, but of those who have principal responsibility".
"I am giving only a possible idea of what might happen...I have to study carefully if we will propose this measure or some other," he said.
The dispute over passports is a symbol of the continued division between the Serb Republic and the Moslem-Croat Federation which constitute postwar Bosnia.
One Bosnian government official said the parties could not agree on whether each of the two halves of Bosnia should be allowed to issue its own passports, the federation opposing such a move.
